metadata.title: Eight Questions on Angels and Man
metadata.latin_title: Libellus octo quaestionum de angelis et homine
metadata.author: Honorius Augustodunensis
known_issues: The printed citation Isaiah, chapter sixty-two, does not match the wording about a new heaven and a new earth; the citation was still spoken as printed, with the discrepancy noted.
The phrase “historialiter, non specialiter” is unusual; I translated the evident contrast as historical versus figurative and noted the uncertainty.

The work’s treatment of unbaptized infants reflects medieval Latin theology; “innocent” in this passage means without personal acts of guilt, not necessarily free from original sin in the author’s system.
The Latin heading “ad beatum vitam” is grammatically irregular; it has been translated according to the evident intended phrase, “ad beatam vitam,” meaning “into blessed life.”
Several biblical allusions are uncited in the printed text, especially in the discussion of Christ reforming the body of our lowliness and the devil’s arrogant speech.
Honorius’s claim that angels have fiery bodies reflects a medieval theological and cosmological position and should not be read as standard later scholastic doctrine.

corrections.original: For the angels, justice would have required something different. Just as that fallen angel exalted himself above all things
corrections.corrected: But it was just that, just as that fallen angel exalted himself above all things
corrections.latin: Justum autem fuit, ut sicut se ille supra omnia extulit
corrections.reason: the opening sentence 'For the angels, justice would have required something different' is an interpretive insertion with no Latin; 'Justum autem fuit, ut …' introduces the comparison directly

corrections.original: so someone from that same angelic order, existing without guilt, would have had to humble himself below all things without seeing the punishment of the fallen angels. He would have had to praise God’s justice
corrections.corrected: so someone from that same number, existing without guilt, should humble himself below all things without seeing the punishment of the fallen, praising God’s justice
corrections.latin: ita aliquis ex numero illo absque culpa existens, non visa poena lapsorum infra omnia se humiliaret, dum justitiam Dei in judiciis suis laudaret
corrections.reason: 'ex numero illo' is 'from that number' (not 'that same angelic order'); 'dum … laudaret' is a subordinate 'while praising', not a second obligation; the modal 'would have had to' overtranslates the result clause

corrections.original: Human beings were destroyed by the first element, that is, in water. Angels, however, were created from the highest element, that is, from fire; and when they sinned, they were hurled down into the second element, that is, into the air.
corrections.corrected: Human beings, made from the first element, were killed in water; angels, however, created from the highest element, that is, from fire, when they sinned were hurled down into the second element, that is, into the air.
corrections.latin: homines de primo elemento, scilicet in aqua sunt necati: angeli vero de summo elemento, scilicet de igne creati, peccantes in secundum elementum, id est in aerem sunt praecipitati
corrections.reason: meaning error: 'de primo elemento' says what humans were made of (earth, the first element — cf. the previous chunk 'terra est prima operum Dei … hominem de terra'), parallel to the angels 'de summo elemento … creati'; the water is where they were killed, not the first element

corrections.original: “Human beings were destroyed…in water” refers to the Flood. Honorius is arranging creation and judgment according to the four elements.
corrections.corrected: Corrected after review: the Latin parallels the two rational creatures by element — humans made from earth (the first element) were killed in water, the element next to earth; angels made from fire (the highest) were cast into air, the element next to fire — so that both, as Honorius says next, will be judged in fire while deified earth is raised above the heavens.
corrections.latin: homines de primo elemento … angeli vero de summo elemento
corrections.reason: explain the elemental scheme behind the corrected sentence

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Whether Man Would Exist If Angels Had Not Fallen
chunks.latin: CAP. I. Utrum homo crearetur, si angelus in coelo perstitisset.
chunks.english: Chapter 1: Whether Man Would Exist If Angels Had Not Fallen

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISCIPULUS. Vellem mihi certa auctoritate monstrari, ac firma ratione probari, utrum homo crearetur, si angelus in coelo perstitisset? cum enim auctoritas cujusdam magni dicat, ut impleretur electorum numerus, homo decimus creatur: videtur ad hoc solum facta multiplicitas hominum, ut impleretur imminuta numerositas angelorum, et sic consequenter ruina angeli fuit causa conditionis hominis.
chunks.english: Student: I would like to be shown by reliable authority, and proved by solid reasoning, whether humanity would have been created if the angel had remained steadfast in heaven. For since the authority of a certain great teacher says that, so the number of the elect might be completed, man was created as the tenth order, it seems that the human race was multiplied only for this purpose: to make up the diminished number of the angels. And so, as a consequence, the fall of the angel would have been the cause of humanity’s creation.
chunks.notes: “A certain great teacher” is identified in the following reply as Gregory, that is, Gregory the Great.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAGISTER. Nihil est aliud auctoritas, quam per rationem probata veritas: et quod auctoritas docet credendum, hoc ratio probat tenendum. Evidens scripturae auctoritas clamat, et perspicax ratio probat: si omnes angeli in coelo permansissent, tamen homo cum omni posteritate sua creatus fuisset. Iste quippe mundus propter hominem est factus; mundus autem est coelum et terra, et universa quae ambitu continentur; et valde absurdum credi videtur, ut stantibus angelis is non crearetur, propter quem universitas creata legitur. Ad hunc errorem removendum sacra Scriptura, futurorum praescia, ante creationem angeli et hominis exorsa est dicens: In principio creavit Deus coelum et terram (Gen. I). Utquid coelum? Ut esset utique habitatio angelorum. Utquid terram? Ut videlicet esset habitatio hominum. Et huic sententiae auctoritas illius magni viri, scilicet Gregorii, non refragatur, sed potius suffragatur: quia nimirum electorum numerus non in solis constitit angelis, sed in angelis simul et hominibus, et quia in novem ordinibus angelorum non erat perfectus numerus electorum, ut hic impleretur numerus, est homo decimus ordo creatus. Quod autem homo cum angelo sit creatus, testatur ipse creator Deus loquens ad Job: Ecce Behemoth, quem feci tecum (Job XL), quod est dicere: Quando feci hominem, feci et angelum. Est autem dualis creatio hominis, una in aeternitate per praedestinationem, altera sub temporalitate per formationem. De creatione praedestinationis scribitur: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram. Et fecit Deus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam (Gen. I). De creatione formationis scriptum est: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terrae et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitae; et factus est in animam viventem (Gen. II). Qui enim manet in aeternum, ait Scriptura, creavit omnia simul (Eccli. XVIII). Omnia creavit simul per materiam, distinxit vero sex diebus per genera, per species, per formas, per numeros. Illi autem sex dies non sunt, ut isti volubiles, intelligendi, sed in aeternitate fixi, ad quorum exemplar isti sunt facti. Et quia senarius numerus perfectus est, ideo sex diebus Deus omnia fecisse legitur: ut operatio Dei perfecta insinuetur; quae in sex partes distinguitur, scilicet in tria elementa et in tria ex his creata. Elementa quippe sunt ignis, aqua, terra; et de igne creati sunt angeli, luminaria et sidera; de terra vero homines, arbores, herbae et animantia; de aquis autem pisces et volucres. Est autem gemina aquarum natura, una crassa semper terrae adhaerens, quae mare dicitur, de qua pisces producti leguntur; altera tenuis a terra suspensa, quae aer dicitur, de qua volucres creatae noscuntur. Quod autem angelus sit principium viarum Dei, scribitur in Job: homo vero ultima factura Dei legitur. Hinc per illum inchoatio, per istum vero consummatio operum Dei innuitur: cui omnis creatura reliqua subjicitur. Igitur sicut nec angeli pro perditis hominibus creantur, ita nec homines pro lapsis angelis creati creduntur, sed proprio loco gloriae possidendo et decimum ordinem electorum implendo. Ideo autem pro perditis angelis dicuntur facti, quia in gloriam, de qua ipsi ceciderant, sunt assumendi: quod nihilominus fieret, si nullus angelorum corruisset. Et ecce nullus hominum adorat angelum, multitudo autem angelorum adorat super se hominem Deum, qui omnia in coelis et in terris restauravit: dum hominem de potestate diaboli in terris liberavit, et in coelis angelis associavit.
chunks.english:
Master: Authority is nothing other than truth that has been proved by reason. And what authority teaches us to believe, reason proves that we must hold. The clear authority of Scripture proclaims it, and sharp reasoning confirms it: even if all the angels had remained in heaven, humanity, with all its descendants, would still have been created.

This world, after all, was made for the human being. And the world means heaven and earth, together with everything contained within their whole expanse. So it seems very absurd to believe that, if the angels had stood firm, the one for whom the whole universe is said to have been created would not himself have been created.

To remove this error, sacred Scripture, foreknowing the future, begins before the creation of angel and human being by saying, as Scripture says in Genesis, chapter one: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Why heaven? Certainly so that it might be the dwelling-place of the angels. Why earth? Clearly so that it might be the dwelling-place of human beings.

And the authority of that great man, Gregory, does not oppose this view. It actually supports it. For the number of the elect did not consist only of angels, but of angels and human beings together. And because the complete number of the elect was not present in the nine orders of angels, humanity was created as the tenth order so that this number might be completed.

That the human being was created along with the angel is testified by God the Creator himself, speaking to Job, in Job, chapter forty: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you.” That is to say: “When I made the human being, I also made the angel.”

Now there is a twofold creation of humanity. One is in eternity, through predestination; the other is within time, through formation. Concerning the creation of predestination it is written in Genesis, chapter one: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” And again: “God made man according to his image and likeness.” Concerning the creation of formation, it is written in Genesis, chapter two: “God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and he became a living soul.” For, as Scripture says in Ecclesiasticus, chapter eighteen, “The one who remains forever created all things together.”

God created all things together as matter, but distinguished them across six days by genera, species, forms, and numbers. Those six days should not be understood as changeable days like ours, but as fixed in eternity; our days were made according to their pattern. And because the number six is a perfect number, Scripture says that God made all things in six days, to suggest that God’s work was perfect. This work is divided into six parts: three elements, and three groups of things created from them.

The elements are fire, water, and earth. From fire were created the angels, the lights, and the stars. From earth were created human beings, trees, plants, and animals. From the waters were created fish and birds. Water, however, has a double nature. One kind is thick and always clings to the earth; it is called the sea, and fish are said to have been brought forth from it. The other kind is thin and suspended above the earth; it is called air, and birds are known to have been created from it.

As for the angel being “the beginning of the ways of God,” this is written in Job. The human being, by contrast, is said to be God’s last work. So by the angel the beginning of God’s works is indicated, and by the human being their completion is indicated; and to the human being all the rest of creation is subjected.

Therefore, just as angels are not created in place of lost human beings, so human beings should not be believed to have been created in place of fallen angels. Rather, they were created to possess their own place of glory and to complete the tenth order of the elect. They are said to have been made “in place of” the lost angels because they are to be taken up into the glory from which those angels fell. But that would still have happened even if none of the angels had fallen.

And notice this: no human being worships an angel, but a multitude of angels worships above themselves the man who is God, the one who restored all things in heaven and on earth. He did this when he freed humanity on earth from the power of the devil and united humanity in heaven with the angels.
chunks.notes: Column markers from the printed edition have not been spoken. The citation “Ecclesiasticus, chapter eighteen” refers to Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus. The phrase “the beginning of the ways of God” alludes to Job chapter forty in the Vulgate context of Behemoth, though the printed text gives no chapter number at that point.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Whether Christ Would Become Incarnate Without Sin
chunks.latin: CAP. II. Utrum Christus incarnaretur, si homo in paradiso perstitisset.
chunks.english: Chapter 2: Whether Christ Would Become Incarnate Without Sin

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISCIPULUS. Quia rationabiliter est probatum, ruinam angeli non fuisse causam creationis hominis, nec hominem pro angelo, sed pro semetipso creatum, vellem item eadem auctoritate, comitante ratione, doceri, utrum Christus incarnaretur, si homo in paradiso perstitisset? Cum enim tota Scriptura clamat, Christum pro humana redemptione in carne venisse; putatur nunquam in carne venisse, si homo non peccasset quem redimeret: et sic videtur peccatum hominis causa fuisse Christi incarnationis. Quod si ita est, tunc illud peccatum non fuit malum, imo magnum bonum, cujus causa Deus factus est homo, consequenter et homo Deus.
chunks.english:
Student: Since it has been reasonably proved that the angel’s fall was not the cause of humanity’s creation, and that the human being was created not in place of the angel but for his own sake, I would likewise like to be taught, with the same authority and with reason accompanying it, whether Christ would have become incarnate if the human being had remained steadfast in paradise.

For since all Scripture proclaims that Christ came in the flesh for human redemption, people think he would never have come in the flesh if there had been no sinful human being for him to redeem. And so human sin seems to have been the cause of Christ’s incarnation. But if that is so, then that sin was not evil. Indeed, it was a great good, because on account of it God became man, and, as a consequence, man became God.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin:
MAG. Peccatum hominis non bonum, sed maximum malum fuisse, clamat totus mundus, cum multis miseriis suis. Unde enim mors cum tot cladibus regnat in mundo, nisi de peccato hominis? et ideo peccatum primi hominis non fuit, causa Christi incarnationis, sed potius fuit causa mortis et damnationis. Causa autem Christi incarnationis fuit praedestinatio humanae deificationis: ab aeterno quippe a Deo erat praedestinatum, ut homo deificaretur, dicente Domino: Pater, dilexisti eos ante constitutionem mundi (Joan. XVII), subaudi, per me deificandos.

Sicut autem Deus est immutabilis, ita et praedestinatio ejus est immutabilis: oportuit ergo hunc incarnari, ut homo posset deificari. Et ideo non sequitur, peccatum fuisse causam ejus incarnationis; sed hoc magis sequitur, peccatum non potuisse propositum Dei immutare de deificatione hominis. Siquidem auctoritas sacrae Scripturae et manifesta ratio declarat, Deum hominem assumpsisse, etiamsi homo nunquam peccasset.

Denique provida Scriptura ante peccatum hominis promittit Christum, dicens: Relinquet homo patrem et matrem, et adhaerebit uxori suae et erunt duo in carne una (Matth. XIX). Haec Apostolus exponit ita, dicens: Sacramentum hoc magnum est, ego dico in Christo et in Ecclesia (Ephes. V). Ecce adhuc nullum peccatum ab homine committitur, et Christi et Ecclesiae conjunctio in una carne praedicatur. Unde idem Apostolus: Deus, inquit, ante mundi constitutionem elegit nos in Christo (Ephes. I). Christus est Deus homo, in quo Deus ante mundi constitutionem praedestinatos ad vitam elegit, quia in Christo nos deificari constituit. Quando enim Deus humanam naturam induit, universa humanitas in electis duntaxat in Deum tunc transit. Sed et primus angelus, qui similitudinem Dei sibi usurpavit, quam solus Filius habuit, dum pulsus de coelo cecidit, Christum Judicem in terra invenit. Adhuc quippe in terrae materie latuit, per quem Pater terram condidit: qui angelum de coelo refugum sub terra mergeret, et hominem humilem de terra super coelum erigeret. Quod autem Christus mortuus est, qui est vita omnium, tres status sunt hominis: unus ante peccatum, in quo mori, et non mori potuit; alter post peccatum in quo mori necesse habuit: tertius, qui erat ei futurus, si tentatus non peccasset, et adhuc post resurrectionem speratur, in quo mori non potuit.

Si ergo Christus in primo statu venisset, nec ipse nec homo unquam moreretur, sed jam deificatus completo numero ordinis decimi angelis associaretur: quod utique factum ita esset, si homo tentatus non peccasset. Sed Christus hominem peccaturum, et per hoc moriturum praescius, ideo in secundo statu venire et mori voluit: ut hominem de morte redimeret, et ad statum vitae reduceret. Et ideo dicitur pro humana redemptione venisse, quia nisi ipse moriendo mortem nostram destrueret, nunquam homo post culpam statum vitae reciperet. Igitur Christi incarnatio fuit humanae naturae deificatio, ejus mors nostrae mortis destructio, ejus resurrectio vitae nostrae reparatio, et hoc modo secundum Apostolum: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo vivificabuntur (I Cor. XV).
chunks.english:
Master: Human sin was not good; it was the greatest evil. The whole world proclaims this with all its many miseries. For why does death reign in the world with so many disasters, if not because of human sin? Therefore the sin of the first human being was not the cause of Christ’s incarnation. Rather, it was the cause of death and condemnation.

The cause of Christ’s incarnation was the predestination of humanity’s deification. From eternity, God had predestined that the human being should be made divine. The Lord says in the Gospel of John, chapter seventeen: “Father, you loved them before the foundation of the world.” Understand this to mean: “you loved those who were to be deified through me.”

Now, just as God is unchangeable, so his predestination is unchangeable. Therefore Christ had to become incarnate so that humanity could be deified. So it does not follow that sin was the cause of his incarnation. What follows instead is this: sin could not change God’s purpose concerning the deification of humanity. Indeed, the authority of sacred Scripture and plain reason both declare that God would have assumed humanity even if humanity had never sinned.

In fact, foreseeing Scripture promises Christ even before human sin when it says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter nineteen: “A man shall leave father and mother, and cling to his wife, and the two shall be in one flesh.” The Apostle explains this by saying in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter five: “This is a great sacrament; I mean it with reference to Christ and the Church.” Look: no sin has yet been committed by the human being, and already the union of Christ and the Church in one flesh is proclaimed.

So the same Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter one: “God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world.” Christ is God and man. In him, before the foundation of the world, God chose for life those whom he had predestined, because God determined that we would be deified in Christ. For when God clothed himself in human nature, then all humanity—at least in the elect—passed over into God.

But also the first angel, who seized for himself the likeness of God that the Son alone possessed, found Christ as judge on earth when he was driven from heaven and fell. For the one through whom the Father founded the earth was still hidden in the material of the earth: the one who would plunge the fugitive angel from heaven beneath the earth, and raise the humble human being from the earth above heaven.

As for the fact that Christ died, though he is the life of all, there are three states of humanity. The first was before sin, when the human being was able to die and also able not to die. The second was after sin, when the human being had to die. The third would have belonged to him if he had been tempted and had not sinned; and this same state is still hoped for after the resurrection, when the human being will not be able to die.

So if Christ had come in the first state, neither he nor humanity would ever have died. Instead, once humanity had been deified and the number of the tenth order had been completed, humanity would have been joined to the angels. That is exactly what would have happened if the human being, when tempted, had not sinned.

But Christ knew beforehand that humanity would sin and, because of that, would die. Therefore he chose to come and die in the second state, so that he might redeem humanity from death and restore humanity to the state of life. For this reason he is said to have come for human redemption: because unless he had destroyed our death by dying, humanity after guilt would never have regained the state of life.

Therefore Christ’s incarnation was the deification of human nature; his death was the destruction of our death; his resurrection was the restoration of our life. And in this way, according to the Apostle in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter fifteen: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.”
chunks.notes: “Deification” translates deificatio, the theological claim that human nature is elevated into participation in God through Christ. The printed citation “the Gospel of Matthew, chapter nineteen” is retained as printed, though the words also echo Genesis chapter two. The printed citation to John chapter seventeen is retained as printed; the wording combines the Johannine theme of love before the foundation of the world with the author’s interpretive gloss.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: How Angels Were Created from Fire
chunks.latin: CAP. III. Quomodo angeli ex igne creati sint.
chunks.english: Chapter 3: How Angels Were Created from Fire

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISC. Haec solutio mihi probabilis videtur, ubi auctoritas rationi, et ratio auctoritati patrocinatur. Sed cum melior sit Spiritus quam corpus, miror cur angelos dixeris de igne creatos. Ignis enim corpus est, angeli vero spiritus sunt: et non video, quo modo melius de deteriori creari praedicetur nisi veris assertionibus comprobetur.
chunks.english: Student: That answer seems plausible to me, because authority supports reason, and reason supports authority. But since spirit is better than body, I am puzzled that you said angels were created from fire. Fire is a body, while angels are spirits. So I do not see how something better can be said to have been created from something worse, unless that claim is proved by solid arguments.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Spiritum de corpore creari dicere insani capitis est, corpus vero de corporibus vel de elementis dicere creari assertio veritatis est. Angelici spiritus, et humanae animae, et informis materia mundi ex nihilo creata sunt; ex informi autem materia elementa discreta sunt, dicente Scriptura: Qui fecit mundum de informi materia. Corpora vero omnia ex quatuor elementis formata sunt, scilicet unumquodque corpus illi elemento specialiter attribuitur, quod in eo plus abundat. Unde dicuntur quaedam corpora coelestia vel ignea, quaedam terrestria, quaedam aquatica, quaedam aerea.
chunks.english: Master: To say that a spirit is created from a body would be the claim of a madman. But to say that a body is created from bodies, or from the elements, is a true assertion. Angelic spirits, human souls, and the unformed matter of the world were created from nothing. From that unformed matter the elements were then separated, as Scripture says, “He made the world from unformed matter.” All bodies, however, were formed from the four elements. That is, each body is assigned especially to the element that predominates in it. That is why some bodies are called heavenly or fiery, some earthly, some watery, and some airy.
chunks.notes: The quotation “He made the world from unformed matter” echoes the Wisdom of Solomon, chapter eleven, verse seventeen, but the printed text gives no explicit reference here.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Animarum corpora sunt terrestria, dicente Scriptura: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terrae (Gen. II), id est corpus hominis. De anima vero subditur: Et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitae (ibid.), de cujus creatione praemittitur: Fecit Deus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam (Gen. I), id est animam hominis. Deus est incorporeus, ita et anima, in qua est imago Dei, est incorporea.
chunks.english: Master: The bodies of souls are earthly bodies, as Scripture says in Genesis, chapter two: “God formed man from the mud of the earth,” meaning the human body. About the soul it then adds, in the same chapter of Genesis: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” Earlier, Scripture had said about the soul’s creation, in Genesis, chapter one: “God made man in his own image and likeness,” meaning the human soul. God is bodiless, and so the soul, in which God’s image exists, is also bodiless.
chunks.notes: The phrase “in the same chapter of Genesis” expands the printed “ibid.” for audio clarity.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: De corporibus animalium dicit Scriptura: Producat terra jumenta et bestias in genere suo (Gen. I), sive corpora jumentorum et bestiarum. De piscibus quoque et volucribus dicit: Producant aquae pisces et volucres in genere suo (ibid.), intellige, piscium corpora et volucrium. Aquae dixit propter geminam naturam aquarum, scilicet crassae uti maris, tenuis uti aeris.
chunks.english: Master: About the bodies of animals, Scripture says in Genesis, chapter one: “Let the earth bring forth cattle and beasts according to their kind,” meaning the bodies of cattle and beasts. About fish and birds it also says, in the same chapter of Genesis: “Let the waters bring forth fish and birds according to their kind.” Understand this to mean the bodies of fish and birds. Scripture says “waters” because water has a double nature: a thick kind, as in the sea, and a thin kind, as in the air.
chunks.notes: The phrase “in the same chapter of Genesis” expands the printed “ibid.” for audio clarity. Honorius follows an older cosmological reading in which the air can be described as a more subtle form of water.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Corpora autem angelicorum spirituum sunt ignea, dicente Scriptura: Qui facit angelos suos spiritus, et ministros suos flammam ignis (Hebr. I); quod est dicere, angelicos spiritus ex nihilo fecit Deus; corpora vero eorum ex igne creavit. De quorum creatione dicit Scriptura: Dixit Deus: Fiat lux (Gen. I), quasi dicat de igne fiant lucida angelorum corpora.
chunks.english: Master: The bodies of angelic spirits, however, are fiery, as Scripture says in the letter to the Hebrews, chapter one: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.” That means this: God made the angelic spirits from nothing, but he created their bodies from fire. Scripture speaks of the creation of those bodies in Genesis, chapter one: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” as if to say, “Let the shining bodies of the angels be made from fire.”
chunks.notes: The quotation in the letter to the Hebrews cites Psalm one hundred three in the Vulgate numbering. Honorius interprets “Let there be light” as referring to the fiery bodies of angels.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Sicut enim rationalis anima corpore vestita dicitur homo, ita intellectualis Spiritus corpore vestitus dicitur angelus. Angeli non in alienis corporibus, sed in propriis olim apparuerunt hominibus, quibus locuti sunt: cum quibus ambulaverunt, cum quibus manducaverunt; quae omnia historialiter, non specialiter facta sunt. Quae tamen corpora pro dispensatione officii sui in diversas species transformare potuerunt: unde aliquando fulgurea facie, aliquando candida veste splendidi visi sunt.
chunks.english: Master: Just as a rational soul clothed with a body is called a human being, so an intellectual spirit clothed with a body is called an angel. In ancient times angels appeared to human beings not in borrowed bodies, but in their own bodies. They spoke with them, walked with them, and ate with them. All these things happened in the historical sense, not merely in a figurative sense. Yet, for the carrying out of their office, angels could transform those bodies into different appearances. That is why they were sometimes seen shining with a lightning-bright face, and sometimes with dazzling white clothing.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin says “historialiter, non specialiter.” The second word is unusual in this contrast; I have translated the evident sense as “not merely in a figurative sense.”

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Et in plerisque sanctorum Scripturis dicuntur daemones per aera discurrere. Non enim spiritus sine corporibus discurrunt, qui illocales sunt. Et notandum, quod Genesis nihil de creatione spirituum dicit, quia non solet de invisibili natura, sed de visibili corporum creatione narrare. Apostolus autem clamat dicens: Sive visibilia, sive invisibilia in coelis et in terris omnia per ipsum facta sunt (Coloss. I). Invisibilia sunt spiritus, visibilia vero corpora eorum.
chunks.english: Master: And in many writings of the saints, demons are said to run about through the air. For spirits without bodies do not run about, since as spirits they are not located in a place. It should also be noticed that Genesis says nothing about the creation of spirits, because Genesis does not usually tell the story of invisible nature, but of the visible creation of bodies. The Apostle proclaims this in Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one: “Whether visible or invisible, in the heavens and on the earth, all things were made through him.” The invisible things are spirits; the visible things are their bodies.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why God Took a Body from Earth, Not Fire
chunks.latin: CAP. IV. Quare creator Deus corpus non de igne, sed de terra sumpsit.
chunks.english: Chapter 4: Why God Took a Body from Earth, Not Fire

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISC. In hac solutione bene concordat ratio auctoritati. Sed cum terra sit infimum elementum, et faex omnium elementorum: ignis vero summum et purissimum elementum, quid rationis habet, quod creator Deus corpus non de igne, sed de terra sumpsit?
chunks.english: Student: In this answer, reason agrees well with authority. But earth is the lowest element, the dregs of all the elements, while fire is the highest and purest element. So what reason is there for the Creator God to have taken a body not from fire, but from earth?

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Centrum est dignius quam circulus: centrum enim immobile figitur, circulus vero mobilis volvitur. Terra enim centrum elementorum est fixa et stabilis: ignis est ut circulus motus instabilis. Et licet omnia elementa in dignitate conditionis sint aequalia; tamen in figuris secundum naturam centrum habet primatum. Terra est centrum mundi, et nutrix omnium animantium: ignis vero peremptor eorum, licet quaedam animalia sint in igne innoxia, ut fertur de Salamandra.
chunks.english: Master: The center is more noble than the circle. The center is fixed and unmoving, while the circle turns and moves. Earth is the center of the elements: fixed and stable. Fire is like a circle: unstable in its motion. And although all the elements are equal in the dignity of their creation, still, when considered according to natural shapes, the center holds first place. Earth is the center of the world and the nurse of all living things. Fire, by contrast, destroys them, although some creatures are said to be unharmed in fire, as people report about the salamander.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Sed et terra est prima operum Dei, dicente Scriptura: In principio tu, Domine, terram fundasti (Psal. CI). Duas rationales creaturas Deus incorporavit de primo et summo elemento, hominem de terra in seipso deificandum, angelum de igne in coelo glorificandum. Unde haec duo elementa immutabuntur in gloriam filiorum Dei, dicente Scriptura: Coelum novum et terram novam faciet Dominus (Isa. LXII); in qua nova terra corpora hominum duntaxat electorum jam deificata ut sol fulgebunt, et corporibus angelorum aequalia erunt: quae ut sol, qui utique est ignis, lucida fulgescunt; quando Christus reformabit corpus humilitatis nostrae configuratum corpori claritatis suae: qui in monte ut sol apparuit, cum in gloria futuri status discipulis apparuit.
chunks.english: Master: Moreover, earth is the first of God’s works, as Scripture says in Psalm one hundred one: “In the beginning, you, Lord, founded the earth.” God gave bodies to two rational creatures from the first and the highest elements: the human being from earth, to be deified in God himself; and the angel from fire, to be glorified in heaven. Therefore these two elements will be changed into the glory of the children of God, as Scripture says in Isaiah, chapter sixty-two: “The Lord will make a new heaven and a new earth.” In that new earth, the bodies of human beings—of the elect alone—will already have been deified and will shine like the sun, and they will be equal to the bodies of the angels. Those angelic bodies shine with a brightness like the sun, which of course is fire. This will happen when Christ reforms the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the body of his glory. Christ appeared like the sun on the mountain, when he appeared to his disciples in the glory of the future state.
chunks.notes: The citation is rendered as printed: Isaiah, chapter sixty-two. The wording “new heaven and new earth” is more closely associated with Isaiah, chapter sixty-five, verse seventeen, and Isaiah, chapter sixty-six, verse twenty-two, as well as Revelation, chapter twenty-one, verse one. The phrase about Christ reforming the body of our lowliness echoes Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter three, verse twenty-one, though no citation is printed.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Praeterea summopere notandum est, quod homines de primo elemento, scilicet in aqua sunt necati: angeli vero de summo elemento, scilicet de igne creati, peccantes in secundum elementum, id est in aerem sunt praecipitati. Ambo adhuc in igne damnabuntur, cum terra in Christo et in electis deificata super coelos exaltabitur.
chunks.english: Master: Besides this, one point must be noticed very carefully. Human beings, made from the first element, were killed in water; angels, however, created from the highest element, that is, from fire, when they sinned were hurled down into the second element, that is, into the air. Both groups will still be condemned in fire, while earth, deified in Christ and in the elect, will be exalted above the heavens.
chunks.notes: “Human beings were destroyed…in water” refers to the Flood. Honorius is arranging creation and judgment according to the four elements.  Corrected after review: the Latin parallels the two rational creatures by element — humans made from earth (the first element) were killed in water, the element next to earth; angels made from fire (the highest) were cast into air, the element next to fire — so that both, as Honorius says next, will be judged in fire while deified earth is raised above the heavens.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why the Angel’s Fall Was Irreparable
chunks.latin: CAP. V. Utrum lapsus angeli ideo irreparabilis fuerit, quia fuit immortalis; hominis contra.
chunks.english: Chapter 5: Whether the Angel’s Fall Was Irreparable Because He Was Immortal, and Man’s the Reverse

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISC. Quorumdam assertio non videtur mihi probabilis, qui dicunt, quod angeli lapsus ideo fuit irreparabilis, quia fuerit immortalis: hominis vero recuperabilis fuit quia mori potuit; cum Deus nihil nisi solam mortem pro reconciliatione utriusque voluerit?
chunks.english: Student: I do not find persuasive the claim made by some people. They say that the angel’s fall was irreparable because the angel was immortal, while the human being’s fall could be repaired because the human being could die. But is it true that God wanted nothing except death alone for the reconciliation of both angels and humans?
chunks.notes: The printed text has “probabilis” divided typographically as “pro babilis.”

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Hoc nec auctoritate probatur, nec ratione roboratur, praesertim cum auctoritas clamet: Deus mortem non fecit, nec laetatur in perditione morientium (Sap. I). Et iterum per prophetam: Nolo mortem peccatoris (Ezech. XXXIII). Ratio autem non sinit ullum contrarium suo opposito jungi: lux enim est tenebris opposita, quas non recipit sed repellit; et vita est morti contraria quam non eligit sed potius exstinguit. Mors quippe est poena peccati, quam homo nunquam subiisset. Deus igitur, qui est vita, nec ab angelo nec ab homine mortem exigit, sed ut sibi et naturae contrariam adimit.
chunks.english: Master: That view is not proved by authority, and it is not strengthened by reason—especially since authority cries out in the Wisdom of Solomon, chapter one: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the dying.” And again, through the prophet in Ezekiel, chapter thirty-three: “I do not desire the death of the sinner.” Reason also does not allow one contrary to be joined to its opposite. Light is opposed to darkness; it does not receive darkness, but drives it away. Life is opposed to death; it does not choose death, but rather destroys it. Death is the punishment of sin, which humanity would never have undergone. Therefore God, who is life, does not demand death from either angel or human being. Instead, because death is contrary both to himself and to nature, he takes it away.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Porro natura rerum exigit, ut quae sunt in universitate discrepantia, per sibi contrarium vel simile fiant consonantia. Ut verbi gratia: voces graves sunt acutis contrariae, et ideo dissona, per easdem autem personantias fiunt consimiles et consonae.
chunks.english: Master: Yet the nature of things requires that whatever is discordant in the universe should be brought into harmony through something contrary to it, or something like it. For example, low notes are contrary to high notes, and for that reason they are dissonant. But through the same musical resonances, they become similar and harmonious.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Homo quippe Deo inobediens, diabolo ad injustitiam factus est obediens, pro qua injustitia debitam mortem incidit: sicque dissonantiam in universitate fecit, dum ad vitam conditus, in morte defecit. Christus vero per contrarium ex simili exhibuit consonantiam, dum Deo ad justitiam factus est obediens, pro qua justitia indebitam mortem sustinuit; sicque mortem destruens hominem de morte redemit.
chunks.english: Master: The human being, by disobeying God, became obedient to the devil in injustice. Because of that injustice, humanity fell under the death it deserved. In this way humanity created discord in the universe: created for life, it collapsed into death. But Christ restored harmony by a contrary action performed from within the same human nature. He became obedient to God in righteousness, and because of that righteousness he endured an undeserved death. Thus, by destroying death, he redeemed humanity from death.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Justitia etenim exigit, ut sicut homo absque peccato conditus, peccando offendit, pro quo poenam mortis pertulit: ita aliquis ex genere ejus absque peccato existens, juste vivendo Deum placaret; cujus causa mortem subiret; per quam consortes Deo reconciliaret. Et quia Christus haec fecit dicitur, quod nihil nisi mortem pro satisfactione voluerit. Ab angelo autem hoc non quaesivit, quia mori non potuit.
chunks.english: Master: Justice required this: just as the human being was created without sin, then offended God by sinning, and therefore suffered the penalty of death; so someone from the human race, existing without sin, had to live righteously and so appease God, undergo death for God’s sake, and through that death reconcile his companions to God. Because Christ did these things, people say that God wanted nothing except death as satisfaction. But God did not seek this from an angel, because an angel could not die.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: Justum autem fuit, ut sicut se ille supra omnia extulit, dum similis Altissimo esse voluit, et ideo infra omnia cecidit: ita aliquis ex numero illo absque culpa existens, non visa poena lapsorum infra omnia se humiliaret, dum justitiam Dei in judiciis suis laudaret, suam vero injustitiam accusaret et hac confessione laudis socios levaret. Sed ille, qui de veritate cecidit, in qua non stetit, adhuc in mendacio, cujus pater est (Joan. VIII), persistit dicens: Mea sunt flumina, et ego feci ea. Ego feci meipsum: ego sum Deus et non homo. Et quia haec vox incorrigibilis est, ideo lapsus ejus irrecuperabilis est.
chunks.english: Master: But it was just that, just as that fallen angel exalted himself above all things when he wanted to be like the Most High, and for that reason fell below all things, so someone from that same number, existing without guilt, should humble himself below all things without seeing the punishment of the fallen, praising God’s justice in his judgments, accuse his own injustice, and by this confession of praise raise up his companions. But the angel who fell away from the truth, in which he did not stand, still persists in the lie whose father he is, as the Gospel of John says in chapter eight. He says: “My rivers are mine, and I made them. I made myself. I am God and not a man.” And because that voice is incorrigible, his fall is therefore beyond recovery.
chunks.notes: The citation to the Gospel of John, chapter eight, refers to the devil as the father of lies. The arrogant sayings that follow combine biblical-sounding phrases, especially from Ezekiel, but no separate citation is printed.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why We Still Die after Christ Defeated Death
chunks.latin: CAP. VI. Quomodo cuncti moriamur, cum mors destructa per Christum praedicetur.
chunks.english: Chapter 6: Why We Still Die after Christ Defeated Death

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISC. Multum me movet quod omnes morimur, cum mors per Christum destructa praedicetur.
chunks.english: Student: It troubles me greatly that all of us still die, even though death is proclaimed to have been destroyed through Christ.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Duae mortes sunt, una corporis, altera animae. Mors corporis separatio est animae a corpore; mors animae est separatio animae a Deo. Sicut ergo mors corporis aufert gaudia mundi, ita mors animae aufert gaudia coeli. Hanc mortem Christus destruxit, dum animas de suppliciis exemptas, gaudiis coeli intulit. Adhuc mortem destruet, dum animas suis corporibus induet, quas postea nulla mors solvet.
chunks.english: Master: There are two deaths: one of the body, and the other of the soul. The death of the body is the separation of the soul from the body. The death of the soul is the separation of the soul from God. Therefore, just as bodily death takes away the joys of the world, so the soul’s death takes away the joys of heaven. Christ destroyed this death when he freed souls from punishments and brought them into the joys of heaven. He will destroy death still further when he clothes souls again with their bodies—bodies that no death will ever separate from them again.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.latin: CAP. VII. Cur resurrectio mortuorum futura sit.
chunks.english: Chapter 7: Why the resurrection of the dead will happen.

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: DISC. Ego credebam resurrectionem in novissimo [Col. 1191C] futuram etiamsi Christus nunquam incarnaretur, ut puta a prophetis praedictam.
chunks.english: Student: I had thought that the resurrection would take place at the last day even if Christ had never become incarnate, since it had been foretold by the prophets.
chunks.notes: The column marker is editorial and is not translated.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Resurrectio non est ideo futura quia a prophetis est praedicta; sed ideo est praedicta quia erat futura. Siquidem prophetica vox nil cogit fieri; sed Spiritus sanctus, cui omnia praeterita et futura sunt praesentia, sua suis praecinuit; quod vel ipse olim facere disposuit, vel homines facturi erant, ut [Col. 1192A] scirent eum inspectorem omnium. Porro resurrectio ideo fit, ut boni plenum gaudium, mali vero plenum supplicium suscipiant: quod ut utrumque non nisi in corpore et anima esse poterit. Justi autem per Christum reconciliati ad vitam assumuntur, qui si non essent reconciliati, nunquam illuc assumerentur. Igitur si Christus in carne non venisset, et sua morte mortem nostram non destruxisset; et sua resurrectione nobis vitam non reddidisset, nullus unquam ad vitam resurgeret: sed omnes pariter in morte remanerent.
chunks.english: Master: The resurrection will not happen because the prophets foretold it. Rather, the prophets foretold it because it was going to happen. A prophetic word does not force anything to take place. Instead, the Holy Spirit, for whom everything past and future is present, announced in advance to his own people what he himself had long ago decided to do, or what human beings were going to do, so that they would know that he sees everything. Now, the resurrection takes place so that the good may receive complete joy, and the evil complete punishment. Neither of these can happen fully except in both body and soul. The righteous, reconciled through Christ, are taken up into life. If they had not been reconciled, they would never be taken up there. So if Christ had not come in the flesh, had not destroyed our death by his own death, and had not restored life to us by his resurrection, no one would ever rise to life. Everyone alike would remain in death.
chunks.notes: The column marker is editorial and is not translated.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why Not Everyone Receives Blessed Life
chunks.latin: CAP. VIII. Cur Deus non omnes homines post resurrectionem ad beatum vitam transferat, maxime infantes, sine culpa decedentes.
chunks.english: Chapter 8: Why God does not bring every human being after the resurrection into blessed life, especially infants who die without fault.
chunks.notes: The Latin heading has “beatum vitam,” grammatically irregular for “beatam vitam”; the translation follows the evident sense.

chunks.speaker: student
chunks.latin: [Col. 1192B] DISC Cum genus humanum ad vitam sit creatum, et per Christum totum sit ad vitam reparatum, valde miror, cur omnes homines post resurrectionem ad beatam vitam non transferat, maxime infantes, qui penitus sine culpa erant
chunks.english: Student: Since the human race was created for life, and through Christ the whole race has been restored for life, I am very puzzled why he does not bring all human beings after the resurrection into blessed life—especially infants, who were entirely without fault.
chunks.notes: The column marker is editorial and is not translated. “Without fault” here refers to the Student’s way of describing infants as lacking personal guilt.

chunks.speaker: master
chunks.latin: MAG. Christus qui est resurrectio et vita, omnes homines ad vitam resuscitabit; et quia ipse est justitia, solos justos in beata vita glorificabit; injustos in miseria relinquet. Et quia ejus occultum judicium exsuperat omnem sensum, quosdam, quos vult, nocentes igne purgatorio purificatos ad gloriam assumit: quosdam, quos vult, innocentes in miseria relinquit, videlicet infantes, quos unda baptismatis non regeneravit. Melius est enim per misericordiam salvari, quam unquam Judicis sententia [Col. 1192C] condemnari. Cur autem hoc faciat, non plus possumus investigare quam illud possumus indagare: cur angelos non fecerit archangelos, vel illos non fecerit thronos; vel feminas non fecerit viros, vel bestias non fecerit aves, vel cur pavoni, tantum decorem pennarum prae caeteris avibus dederit et multa his similia Omnia enim quaecunque voluit, fecit et facit (Psal. CXIII).
chunks.english: Master: Christ, who is the resurrection and the life, will raise all human beings to life. And because he himself is justice, he will glorify only the righteous in blessed life, and will leave the unrighteous in misery. And because his hidden judgment surpasses every human understanding, he takes some guilty people, purified by purgatorial fire, into glory, as he chooses. And he leaves some innocent people in misery, as he chooses—namely, infants whom the water of baptism has not regenerated. For it is better to be saved by mercy than ever to be condemned by the sentence of the Judge. Why he does this is no more something we can search out than we can discover why he did not make angels into archangels, or those beings into thrones; why he did not make women into men, or beasts into birds; why he gave the peacock such beauty of feathers beyond the other birds; and many similar things. As Scripture says in Psalm one hundred thirteen: “He has done, and does, whatever he has willed.”
chunks.notes: The column marker is editorial and is not translated. The citation is printed only as “Psalm one hundred thirteen,” without a verse number. In Vulgate numbering, the quoted phrase corresponds to Psalm one hundred thirteen; in many modern Bibles it appears in Psalm one hundred fifteen, verse three. The phrase “those beings into thrones” refers to angels not made into the angelic order called “thrones.”
